items.stem: A file server replicates every write to a second machine in another rack. An operator deletes a directory by mistake, and the deletion appears on the second machine within seconds. Which safeguard was missing?

options.text: A backup, an independent copy from which the deleted directory can be restored.
options.why: A backup is a separate copy taken at a point in time, so a deletion made after it does not reach it.

options.text: More replication targets, so at least one copy escapes the deletion.
options.why: Replication faithfully copies deletions to every target, so adding targets multiplies the deletion rather than escaping it.

options.text: A RAID array, so the directory survives the loss of any single disk.
options.why: RAID protects against disk failure, not against a delete the filesystem was asked to perform.

options.text: Nothing — replication to a second machine is a backup.
options.why: A common belief, and the reason this pair is examinable: replication gives availability, not recoverability.

items.rationale: A backup is an independent copy kept so data can be restored after loss, corruption or deletion. Replication and RAID both keep a second copy live, and both apply the destructive operation to that copy as faithfully as to the first. Common tools for taking that independent copy are `tar` for archiving and `rsync` for file-level copies.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 states that HA "cannot be a replacement for a solid backup strategy, as a corruption of data on a system may propagate through an HA system", and that "without a backup of the system separate from the system itself, recovery may not be possible" — the independent copy is the missing safeguard. o2 is false for the same reason: a propagating operation reaches every target, so target count does not help. o3 is true as written — RAID addresses disk failure, not a delete the filesystem was instructed to perform. o4 is the documented misconception and is false. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: You need to copy a large directory tree to a backup host nightly, transferring only the files that changed since the previous run. Which tool is designed for that?

options.text: `rsync` run nightly against the backup host
options.why: It compares source and destination and transfers only differing files, which is what makes repeated runs cheap.

options.text: `tar` writing a fresh archive on every run
options.why: It bundles files into a single archive but has no notion of what the destination already holds, so every run copies everything.

options.text: A filesystem snapshot of the source volume
options.why: A local snapshot stays on the same storage as the original and never moves data to the backup host.

options.text: Continuous replication to the backup host
options.why: That keeps a live mirror rather than a nightly independent copy, and propagates deletions immediately.

items.rationale: `rsync` exists precisely for repeated directory-tree copies: it determines what differs and sends only that. `tar` creates an archive and is the right tool for bundling, not for incremental transfer.

verification.reasoning: Refuted on sourcing: the item cited only NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, which says nothing about rsync or tar. rsync(1) states it "is famous for its delta-transfer algorithm, which reduces the amount of data sent over the network by sending only the differences between the source files and the existing files in the destination" and that it "can copy locally, to/from another host over any remote shell", which is exactly the key. source_ids now carry rsync-man and gnu-tar-manual alongside the NIST backup-policy citation. Key and all three distractors re-checked after the change: o2 (tar has no notion of destination state), o3 (a local snapshot moves nothing off the source storage) and o4 (continuous replication is a live mirror) are each true and none answers the stem.

items.stem: A site takes a full backup on Sunday and a differential backup every weekday night. The server fails on Thursday morning. Which sets must be restored?

options.text: Sunday's full, then Wednesday's differential only.
options.why: A differential holds everything changed since the last full, so only the most recent one is needed.

options.text: Sunday's full, then Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday in order.
options.why: That is the restore sequence for incrementals, each of which holds only what changed since the previous backup.

options.text: Wednesday's differential only.
options.why: A differential is not self-contained; without the full it has no baseline to apply changes to.

options.text: Sunday's full only, since differentials are for retention rather than restore.
options.why: Differentials are restore inputs, and skipping them discards every change made since Sunday.

items.rationale: The distinction lives on the restore side. A differential accumulates all changes since the last full, so a restore needs the full plus one differential. An incremental holds only what changed since the previous backup of any kind, so a restore needs the full plus every incremental in sequence.

verification.reasoning: Key holds verbatim against NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "Restoring from a differential backup may require fewer media than an incremental backup because only the full backup media and the last differential media would be needed." o2 states the incremental restore sequence, which the same section describes ("media from different backup operations may be required"), and is therefore true but not the answer to a differential schedule. o3 is false — a differential stores files changed since the last full and has no baseline without it. o4 is false; the same section makes differentials restore inputs. No second defensible answer.

items.stem: An administrator takes an LVM snapshot before a risky upgrade. The underlying physical volume then fails outright. What is the state of the snapshot?

options.text: Lost with the volume, because a local snapshot is stored on the same storage as the original.
options.why: A local snapshot is a view into the same underlying storage, so it does not survive that storage failing.

options.text: Intact, because a snapshot is an independent copy of the data held apart from the original volume.
options.why: That describes a backup; independence from the original storage is exactly what a local snapshot lacks.

options.text: Intact, because snapshots are always written to separate storage.
options.why: True of typical cloud provider snapshots, but not of local LVM or filesystem snapshots.

options.text: Intact, because RAID parity reconstructs it from the surviving disks.
options.why: RAID is a separate mechanism and is not implied by taking a snapshot.

items.rationale: A snapshot is a point-in-time view of a volume. Local snapshots live alongside the original, so losing the volume loses them, which is why they are not an independent copy. Cloud provider snapshots are typically written to separate storage and do survive deletion of the source volume — the distinction is where the snapshot is stored, not the word itself.

verification.reasoning: Refuted on sourcing: the only citation was the AWS EBS snapshots page, which describes provider snapshots stored in S3 and says nothing about LVM. lvcreate(8) settles the key directly — snapshot space "is allocated from space in the VG", and standard LV allocation "requires allocating logical extents from the VG's free physical extents" — so a snapshot of a volume whose physical volume fails sits on that same failed storage. man-lvcreate-8 added to source_ids. Re-checked after the change: o2 describes a backup, not a local snapshot; o3's why is true of AWS EBS ("Snapshots are stored in Amazon S3") but not of LVM, which is the point of the item; o4 is a mechanism not implied by taking a snapshot. None of the three is also correct.

items.stem: Which single property separates a backup from a local volume snapshot?

options.text: The backup is independent of the original storage; the local snapshot is not.
options.why: Independence from the source storage is the axis the whole comparison turns on.

options.text: The backup is taken at a point in time; the snapshot is continuous.
options.why: Both are point-in-time; continuous copying describes replication instead.

options.text: The backup can be restored; the snapshot cannot be restored from.
options.why: A snapshot can be rolled back to; the limitation is its dependence on the same storage.

options.text: The backup is compressed; the snapshot is stored uncompressed.
options.why: Compression is an implementation detail of either and settles nothing about recoverability.

items.rationale: Both capture a moment. Only the backup is stored independently of the volume it came from, which is what lets it survive the loss of that volume. Cloud snapshots blur this because their storage is separate — the axis is still independence, not the label.

verification.reasoning: Refuted on sourcing alongside snapshot.01: the "local snapshot is not independent" half of the key was carried by the AWS EBS page, which does not discuss local snapshots. lvcreate(8) supplies it (snapshot space allocated from the VG); NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 supplies the backup half ("It is good business practice to store backed-up data offsite"). man-lvcreate-8 added. Re-checked: o2 is false — the AWS page calls a snapshot a "point-in-time" copy, so both are point-in-time and continuous copying is replication; o3 is false, a snapshot can be restored from, its limit is where it lives; o4 is false, compression is orthogonal. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A database is replicated synchronously to a second data centre. A bad migration script corrupts a table at 09:00. What does replication give you at 09:05?

options.text: A second copy of the corrupted table, available for service.
options.why: Replication copies whatever the primary wrote, including the corruption, and does so promptly.

options.text: The table as it stood before the migration, held on the replica.
options.why: That is what a backup or a point-in-time copy provides; a replica tracks the primary rather than lagging it deliberately.

options.text: An automatic rollback once the replica detects the inconsistency.
options.why: Replication has no notion of whether a change was intended and performs no such rollback.

options.text: Protection, because replication satisfies the off-site requirement of the 3-2-1 rule.
options.why: Distance is not the issue here; the replica is off-site and still corrupt.

items.rationale: Replication continuously copies data to another system for availability. Its fidelity is the point and the problem: it reproduces deletions and corruption as faithfully as legitimate writes, which is why it is not a backup.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "a corruption of data on a system may propagate through an HA system, making the system unusable" — the replica at 09:05 holds the corrupted table and is available. o2 is false: a synchronous replica tracks the primary and holds no earlier state. o3 is false; replication carries no notion of intent and performs no rollback. o4 is false as an inference — the copy is off-site and corrupt, so distance did not help. None of the three is also correct.

items.stem: Which requirement is replication the appropriate answer to?

options.text: Service must continue from a second site if the primary becomes unavailable.
options.why: Keeping a current copy live elsewhere is exactly what replication is for.

options.text: A file deleted by an operator last Tuesday must still be recoverable from a retained copy.
options.why: Reaching back to a past state needs a retained independent copy, not a current mirror.

options.text: Restores must be proven to work against a published schedule each quarter.
options.why: That is a testing obligation and is satisfied by exercising restores, not by copying data.

options.text: Storage cost must fall as data ages beyond its useful window.
options.why: That is addressed by retention policy and tiering, which replication does not provide.

items.rationale: Replication answers an availability question — can something else serve if this fails. It does not answer a recoverability question, because it holds only the current state and propagates every change to it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 lists data mirroring and offsite database replication among the high-availability and redundancy options for high-impact systems, i.e. the answer to "can something else serve if this fails". o2 is a recoverability requirement and needs a retained copy, which the same document places in backup and offsite storage. o3 is a testing obligation. o4 is a retention and cost question. Each distractor states a true fact and none is answered by replication.

items.stem: What does the 3-2-1 backup rule prescribe?

options.text: Three copies of the data, on two types of media, with one held off-site.
options.why: That is the rule as stated: copy count, media diversity, and one copy at a distance.

options.text: Three full backups, two differentials, and one incremental each week.
options.why: The rule says nothing about backup types or schedule; it constrains copies, media and location.

options.text: Three sites, two of them warm, and one hot.
options.why: Site tiers are a separate decision driven by recovery time, not by this rule.

options.text: Three restore tests a year, two of them full, and one tabletop.
options.why: Testing cadence is a distinct practice and is not what the numbers refer to.

items.rationale: Three copies, two media types, one off-site. It is a compact expression of what actually makes backups survive a disaster: more than one copy, not all vulnerable to the same failure mode, and not all in the same building.

verification.reasoning: Key holds verbatim against the CISA/US-CERT paper: "3 – Keep 3 copies of any important file: 1 primary and 2 backups. 2 – Keep the files on 2 different media types to protect against different types of hazards. 1 – Store 1 copy offsite." o2, o3 and o4 each attach the numerals to backup type, site tier and test cadence respectively; the paper attaches them to copies, media and location, so all three are false and each why states that correctly.

items.stem: Nightly backup jobs have reported success for two years. What does that establish about the organisation's ability to recover?

options.text: Nothing about recovery, only that the jobs ran without reporting an error.
options.why: A successful write says nothing about whether the resulting copy can be read back into a working system.

options.text: That the recovery time objective is being met.
options.why: A recovery time target can only be evidenced by timing an actual restore.

options.text: That the disaster recovery plan is validated.
options.why: Validating the plan requires rehearsing the procedure and the roles, not reading a job log.

options.text: That the data is recoverable, since a successful backup implies a successful restore.
options.why: This is the assumption the practice exists to break; media, encryption keys and tooling all fail silently.

items.rationale: Restore testing periodically proves a backup can actually be restored. Until that is done, an untested backup is an assumption rather than a safeguard — and it is the step most commonly skipped.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 requires backup media to be tested (it directs the coordinator to determine "how often backup media should be tested") and separates testing, which "validates recovery capabilities", from the backup operation itself. o2 is false: an RTO is a duration and only a timed recovery evidences it. o3 is false; validating a plan is the TT&E activity, not a job log. o4 is the documented misconception. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A team restores a database backup into an isolated environment each quarter and checks the row counts. Which obligation does this satisfy?

options.text: Restore testing — proving the backup can be read back and yields usable data.
options.why: Reading the copy back and confirming its contents is exactly what this practice requires.

options.text: A disaster recovery drill, since the recovery procedure has been exercised.
options.why: A drill rehearses the whole plan and the people in it, not one artefact restoring correctly.

options.text: The off-site requirement, since the isolated environment is elsewhere.
options.why: Where the test runs is incidental; the off-site requirement is about where copies are kept.

options.text: The retention policy, since quarterly checks confirm the copies still exist.
options.why: Retention governs how long copies are kept, which existence checks alone do not establish.

items.rationale: Restoring into an isolated environment and verifying the result is restore testing. It proves the artefact works. It does not prove the organisation can execute its recovery plan under pressure, which is a separate exercise.

verification.reasoning: Key holds — reading the copy back and confirming its contents is precisely the media-testing and validation-data-testing activity NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 describes ("testing and validating recovered data to ensure that data files or databases have been recovered completely"). o2 is false: a drill exercises the plan and the people, and the same document's TT&E section keeps exercises distinct from testing an artefact. o3 and o4 are false and their whys are accurate about what off-site storage and retention govern.

items.stem: A retention policy keeps daily backups for 14 days and nothing longer. A corruption introduced 40 days ago is discovered today. What is the consequence?

options.text: No clean copy remains, because every retained backup already contains the corruption.
options.why: Retention sets how far back recovery can reach, and 14 days does not reach 40.

options.text: The oldest retained backup predates the corruption and can therefore be restored intact.
options.why: The oldest retained copy is 14 days old, which is well after the corruption occurred.

options.text: Replication to the standby site preserves an uncorrupted version.
options.why: Replication tracks the current state and would have copied the corruption when it happened.

options.text: The recovery point objective determines whether the data is recoverable.
options.why: That target describes tolerable data loss in a recovery, not how far back copies survive.

items.rationale: Retention balances recovery reach against storage cost and compliance obligations. It sets the oldest state you can return to, so a fault discovered outside the window is unrecoverable regardless of how reliable the backups were.

verification.reasoning: Key holds on the arithmetic the stem supplies: a 14-day window cannot reach a fault introduced 40 days ago. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 places media rotation frequency and backup scope in backup policy, which is what sets that reach. o2 is false — the oldest retained copy is 14 days old, well after the corruption. o3 is false; replication would have copied the corruption when it happened, per the propagation sentence in the same document. o4 is false: the RPO "is a factor of how much data loss the mission/business process can tolerate", not how far back copies survive. Noted: NIST addresses retention only as rotation frequency inside backup policy, so this citation is thin, but nothing in the item is attributed to it falsely.

items.stem: A service states a four-hour recovery point objective and a one-hour recovery time objective. What do those two figures constrain?

options.text: At most four hours of data may be lost, and service must be back within one hour.
options.why: The recovery point bounds data loss looking backwards; the recovery time bounds the outage looking forwards.

options.text: Service must be back within four hours, and at most one hour of data may be lost.
options.why: This swaps the two, which is the single most common error on this pair.

options.text: Backups run every four hours and drills run hourly.
options.why: Backup frequency follows from the recovery point target but is not what the figure states.

options.text: The system tolerates four hours of downtime a year at one-hour granularity.
options.why: That describes an availability budget, which is a different measure entirely.

items.rationale: The recovery point objective looks backwards to the last good copy and therefore dictates backup frequency. The recovery time objective looks forwards to service restoration and therefore dictates recovery method and standby capacity. Reversing them is the classic mistake.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against both glossary entries. RPO: "The point in time to which data must be recovered after an outage"; SP 800-34 Rev. 1 adds that it "is a factor of how much data loss the mission/business process can tolerate". RTO: "the overall length of time an information system's components can be in the recovery phase before negatively impacting the organization's mission". So four hours bounds data loss and one hour bounds the outage. o2 swaps them and is false. o3 is false — backup frequency follows from the RPO but is not what the figure states. o4 describes an availability budget. No second defensible answer.

items.stem: A team must reduce its recovery point objective from 24 hours to 1 hour. Which change achieves that?

options.text: Capture backups or log shipments at least hourly.
options.why: The tolerable data loss is bounded by the interval between recoverable copies.

options.text: Provision a hot site so recovery completes faster.
options.why: Faster recovery shortens the outage, not the amount of data lost before it began.

options.text: Automate failover so the standby takes over unattended.
options.why: Automated failover reduces time to restore service rather than the recovery point.

options.text: Extend retention so more historical copies are available.
options.why: Retention extends how far back you can reach, not how recent the newest copy is.

items.rationale: The recovery point objective is a statement about acceptable data loss, and the only lever on it is how often a recoverable copy is made. Everything that speeds up recovery moves the recovery time objective instead.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 defines the RPO as the point to which data can be recovered "(given the most recent backup copy of the data)", so the interval between recoverable copies is the only lever on it. o2 and o3 both shorten the outage and therefore move the RTO, which the same section defines as time unavailable; their whys say exactly that and are true. o4 is false — retention governs reach backwards, not the age of the newest copy. None of the three also answers the stem.

items.stem: A service carries a 30-minute recovery time objective. Which recovery arrangement is consistent with it?

options.text: A hot site with equipment running and recent data already loaded.
options.why: Only an already-equipped, already-loaded facility can take over inside half an hour.

options.text: A warm site holding hardware, with data restored from backup when needed.
options.why: The restore step alone will normally exceed thirty minutes.

options.text: A cold site with space, power and environmental control provisioned.
options.why: Hardware would have to be procured and installed first, which takes days or longer.

options.text: Nightly off-site tape rotation with a documented restore procedure.
options.why: Retrieving and restoring media is measured in hours, not in the stated window.

items.rationale: The recovery time objective dictates the recovery method and the standby capacity that must be paid for. Matching a site tier to a stated recovery time is a textbook question shape: the tighter the target, the more of the destination must already be running.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "Hot sites are locations with fully operational equipment and capacity to quickly take over system operations", with "Short" setup time in Table 3-3; the CSRC glossary calls a hot site "a fully operational offsite data processing facility equipped with hardware and software". o2 is false and its why is true: a warm site's "equipment is not loaded with the software or data required to operate the system", so a restore must run first (Table 3-3 setup time: Medium). o3 is false — a cold site has "no equipment or telecommunications established or in place" and Long setup time. o4 is false; media retrieval and restore is not a half-hour operation.

items.stem: Which measurement would demonstrate that a stated recovery time objective is actually achievable?

options.text: Timing a rehearsed recovery from failure to service restored.
options.why: The target is a duration, so only a timed end-to-end recovery evidences it.

options.text: Confirming the age of the most recent restorable copy.
options.why: That evidences the recovery point instead, which measures data loss rather than elapsed time.

options.text: Counting how many components have a redundant pair.
options.why: Redundancy reduces the chance of an outage without establishing how long recovery takes.

options.text: Reviewing the retention schedule for the backup sets.
options.why: Retention concerns how long copies persist, which is unrelated to restoration speed.

items.rationale: A recovery time objective is a claim about elapsed time from failure to restored service. The only evidence for it is a timed rehearsal; everything else evidences a different property.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. The RTO is defined as a length of time, so the only direct evidence is a timed end-to-end recovery; NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 assigns exactly that role to testing, which "validates recovery capabilities". o2 evidences the recovery point, not elapsed time. o3 is true about redundancy and irrelevant to duration. o4 is true about retention and irrelevant to duration. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: Which of these belongs in a disaster recovery plan rather than in a runbook for routine operations?

options.text: The order of system restoration and who is authorised to declare a disaster.
options.why: Sequencing and decision authority under a major failure are what this document exists to fix in advance.

options.text: The procedure for rotating an expiring TLS certificate.
options.why: That is scheduled maintenance and does not involve recovering from a major failure.

options.text: The organisation's strategy for continuing to trade during a disruption.
options.why: That is the broader continuity discipline, of which IT recovery is one component.

options.text: The load balancer's health-check interval for a failing node.
options.why: That is an availability mechanism operating within a site rather than a recovery procedure.

items.rationale: A disaster recovery plan is the documented, tested procedure for restoring service after a major failure — including who does what and in what order. Its distinguishing content is the sequencing and the decision rights, which are precisely what nobody can improvise at the time.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 directly: section 4.2.1 states that when an activation criterion is met "the designated authority should activate the plan", and section 4.3.1 is titled Sequence of Recovery Activities. Decision authority and restoration order are therefore plan content, not routine-runbook content. o2 is scheduled maintenance. o3 is the BCP, which "focuses on sustaining an organization's mission/business processes during and after a disruption". o4 is a within-site availability mechanism. Each why states a true fact.

items.stem: An auditor asks for evidence that a disaster recovery plan is more than a document. What satisfies the request?

options.text: Records of exercises in which the plan was followed and its gaps recorded.
options.why: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 has testing validate recovery capabilities and exercises identify planning gaps, so the exercise record is the evidence.

options.text: Signed acknowledgements from every named role confirming they have read the current version.
options.why: Acknowledgement shows awareness but never shows the procedure works.

options.text: Backup job logs showing two years of successful runs.
options.why: Successful writes evidence neither restoration nor the plan around it.

options.text: A diagram of the standby site's network topology.
options.why: Documentation of the destination says nothing about whether the procedure was exercised.

items.rationale: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 makes testing, training and exercises a step of the contingency planning process in its own right: testing validates recovery capabilities and exercising the plan identifies planning gaps. The glossary definition of a disaster recovery plan does not itself use the word tested, so what evidences a working plan is the exercise record rather than the definition. A plan nobody has rehearsed is a proposal: it has never met the conditions it was written for, and the gaps it contains are still unknown.

verification.reasoning: Refuted: the rationale claimed "The definition carries the word tested". None of the five CSRC glossary definitions of disaster recovery plan contains the word tested — they read "a predetermined set of instructions or procedures..." and "a written plan for recovering one or more information systems at an alternate facility". Claim true, citation wrong: the testing obligation is in NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 ("Testing validates recovery capabilities, whereas training prepares recovery personnel for plan activation and exercising the plan identifies planning gaps"). Rationale and the key's why rewritten to attribute it there. Re-checked after the change: o2 (acknowledgement is not evidence of function), o3 (successful writes evidence neither restoration nor the plan) and o4 (topology documentation is not an exercise record) are each true and none is also correct.

items.stem: How do business continuity and disaster recovery relate to each other?

options.text: Disaster recovery is one component of business continuity, which is broader.
options.why: Continuity covers keeping the organisation operating; IT recovery is one part of that.

options.text: Business continuity is the IT subset of the wider disaster recovery discipline.
options.why: This inverts the containment; the technical procedure sits inside the organisational one.

options.text: They are two names for the same set of activities.
options.why: They differ in scope, and treating them as synonyms is what the comparison tests.

options.text: Business continuity applies during an incident; disaster recovery applies afterwards.
options.why: Both span the incident and its aftermath; the difference is breadth, not timing.

items.rationale: Business continuity is the discipline of keeping the organisation operating through disruption — staff, premises, suppliers, communications and systems. Disaster recovery is the part of that concerned with restoring IT service. The axis is scope: one contains the other.

verification.reasoning: Key holds on scope. The CSRC glossary BCP is "a predetermined set of instructions or procedures that describe how an organization's mission/business processes will be sustained during and after a significant disruption"; NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 section 2.2.6 makes the DRP "an information system-focused plan designed to restore operability of the target system... at an alternate site" that "may support a BCP or COOP plan by recovering supporting systems for mission/business processes". The narrower discipline serving the broader one is what the key asserts. o2 inverts that and is false. o3 is false; the two differ in scope. o4 is false — the BCP definition explicitly spans "during and after", so timing is not the axis. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A flood closes an office for a month. Which concern belongs to business continuity rather than to disaster recovery?

options.text: Where staff will work and how customers will be told.
options.why: People, premises and communications are continuity concerns beyond restoring systems.

options.text: Which systems are restored first and in what order.
options.why: Restoration sequencing is the technical recovery procedure.

options.text: How much data was lost between the last copy and the flood.
options.why: That quantity is bounded by the recovery point objective, a recovery measure.

options.text: Whether the standby site can carry production load.
options.why: Standby capacity is part of the technical recovery arrangement.

items.rationale: Continuity asks whether the organisation can keep operating; recovery asks whether the systems can be brought back. A month without an office raises questions no restore procedure answers.

verification.reasoning: Key holds: premises, staff and customer communication are mission/business-process continuity, which the BCP definition covers and which no system restoration answers. o2 is the DRP's Sequence of Recovery Activities. o3 is bounded by the RPO, "a factor of how much data loss the mission/business process can tolerate". o4 is standby capacity, an alternate-site decision. All three whys are true and all three sit on the recovery side of the line.

items.stem: A cluster survives the loss of any single node without interruption. What does that arrangement not provide?

options.text: Recovery if the whole site or system is lost.
options.why: Availability within a site does not address losing the site itself.

options.text: Continued service when one node fails.
options.why: That is precisely what the arrangement does provide.

options.text: Automatic transfer of work away from the failed node.
options.why: Shifting work off a failed member is part of how the cluster stays available.

options.text: A documented order for bringing systems back after a major failure.
options.why: That is the recovery plan, which is a document rather than something a cluster provides.

items.rationale: High availability avoids downtime from component failure within a site. Disaster recovery restores service after a site or system is lost. They solve different problems and are not substitutes — a perfectly available cluster in a flooded building is unavailable.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "HA can be implemented at a single site, with all system redundancy resident at that site. This will keep the system running at an HA level as long as there is no interruption of the facility housing the system." Losing the site is exactly what the cluster does not cover. o2 and o3 name things the cluster does provide, and their whys say so. o4 is a document, not a property of a cluster. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A budget holder proposes cancelling the standby site because the production cluster is already highly available. What is the flaw?

options.text: The cluster protects against component failure, not against losing the location it sits in.
options.why: The two mechanisms address different failure scopes, so one cannot replace the other.

options.text: There is no flaw, since a highly available cluster already makes a separate recovery site unnecessary.
options.why: This is the substitution the comparison exists to prevent.

options.text: The cluster cannot meet a recovery point objective of any length.
options.why: Data loss targets are governed by copy frequency and are not a property of clustering.

options.text: Clusters are unable to fail back once a node returns to health.
options.why: Returning work to a recovered member is ordinary cluster behaviour.

items.rationale: Availability engineering removes single points of failure inside a site. Recovery engineering assumes the site is gone. Cancelling the second because the first exists leaves the organisation exposed to exactly the event the second was bought for.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against the same passage — HA holds only "as long as there is no interruption of the facility housing the system", and the document instructs that HA processes be extended to an alternate location. o2 is the documented misconception and is false. o3 is false: copy frequency, not clustering, governs the recovery point. o4 is false; returning work to a recovered member is ordinary cluster behaviour. None is also correct.

items.stem: Two application servers are load balanced, each with dual power supplies, and both draw from one switch. Where is the single point of failure?

options.text: The switch, because no duplicate exists for it.
options.why: It is the one component whose loss stops the service, having no counterpart.

options.text: The application servers, because two is too few for redundancy.
options.why: Two is sufficient for the service to survive losing one of them.

options.text: The dual power supplies, because two units inside one chassis do not count as redundancy.
options.why: Each server is described as carrying two supplies, so the loss of one supply stops nothing.

options.text: The load balancer, because balancing implies a single decision point.
options.why: Nothing in the description says the balancer is unduplicated, whereas the switch plainly is.

items.rationale: The practice is duplicating components so that no single failure stops the service, and then identifying where no such duplicate exists. The answer is always the component with a count of one on the path every request takes.

verification.reasoning: Refuted on the second-defensible-answer test: o3 read "The power supplies, because they share the same building feed", importing a premise the stem never gives and naming something that would genuinely be a single point of failure if granted; its why then rebutted a different claim than the option made. Rewritten to "The dual power supplies, because two units inside one chassis do not count as redundancy", which the stem contradicts directly. Key re-checked: the switch is the one component on every request path with a count of one, which is the practice NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 names as "identify single points of failure" and "implement redundancy in critical components". o2 and o4 re-checked and remain false, o4 correctly noting the stem never says the balancer is unduplicated.

items.stem: An organisation has failed over to its standby site three times and never returned to the primary without an unplanned outage. Which step is under-tested?

options.text: Failback, returning to the primary once it is healthy.
options.why: The failovers completed each time and the unplanned outages fell on the return leg, so that leg is what has never been proven.

options.text: Failover, since three activations indicate an unreliable trigger.
options.why: The failovers succeeded; the outages occurred on the return leg.

options.text: Restore testing, since the standby data must have been wrong.
options.why: Nothing indicates a bad restore; the fault appears when moving back.

options.text: Retention, since older copies were needed on each return.
options.why: Retention governs how long copies persist and is not exercised by a site switch.

items.rationale: Failover switches service onto a standby when the primary fails; failback returns it once the primary is healthy. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery documents failback as a separate operation with its own mechanism — reverse replication of the recovery instances back to the source servers — so a rehearsal of the outbound half establishes nothing about the return leg.

verification.reasoning: Refuted twice over. Sourcing: NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 was the only citation and the document never uses the word failback. Content: the key's why asserted failback "is routinely rehearsed least and fails most", a claim no source establishes. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery documents failback as its own process — "the process of returning your workloads from the recovery environment on AWS back to your original source infrastructure after the disaster has been resolved" with its own reverse-replication mechanism — which is the sourceable point. aws-drs-failback added; the why now reasons from the stem (the failovers completed, the outages fell on the return leg) and the rationale from the AWS definition. Re-checked: o2 is false because the failovers succeeded, o3 false because nothing indicates a bad restore, o4 false because a site switch does not exercise retention.

items.stem: During failback from a standby that has been serving writes for two days, what must be handled before the primary resumes service?

options.text: The writes accumulated on the standby must be reconciled onto the primary.
options.why: The primary's data is two days stale, so resuming without reconciliation loses those writes.

options.text: Nothing — the primary holds the authoritative copy by definition.
options.why: Authority moved with service; treating the stale primary as authoritative discards real data.

options.text: The recovery time objective must be lengthened to permit the switch.
options.why: Targets describe requirements and do not resolve a data divergence.

options.text: The standby's snapshots must be deleted to avoid conflicts.
options.why: Removing point-in-time copies destroys evidence and resolves no divergence.

items.rationale: While the standby serves, it becomes the system of record. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery describes failback as returning workloads to the original source infrastructure and assists it by replicating data from the recovery instances back to the source servers, so failback has a data problem at its centre rather than merely a routing one — which is why it is harder than failover and more often goes wrong.

verification.reasoning: Refuted on sourcing: the key claim that writes accumulated on the standby must be reconciled onto the primary was cited to NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1, which never mentions failback. AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery states it "assists with failback by replicating data from recovery instances back to your source servers", and its failback table lists reverse replication as the mechanism — the key exactly. aws-drs-failback added and the rationale re-attributed. Re-checked: o2 is the documented misconception and false, since authority moved with service; o3 is false, an objective is a requirement and resolves no divergence; o4 is false and destructive. None is also correct.

items.stem: In common usage, what do MTTR and MTBF describe?

options.text: How long repair typically takes, and how often failures typically occur.
options.why: The two terms address repair duration and failure frequency respectively.

options.text: How much data may be lost, and how long restoration may take.
options.why: Those are the recovery point and recovery time objectives, which are targets rather than observed averages.

options.text: How many copies are kept, and for how long.
options.why: That describes retention policy, which is unrelated to either measure.

options.text: How quickly a standby activates, and how quickly the primary returns.
options.why: Those describe failover and failback timing rather than these two metrics.

items.rationale: Mean time to repair is how quickly service returns; mean time between failures is how often it breaks. Both are observed averages describing past behaviour, which is what separates them from objectives, which are targets set in advance.

verification.reasoning: The concept is on the sourcing waiver list, so the item may only turn on a definition every consensus source agrees about, and it does: MTTR is repair duration and MTBF is failure frequency, and the stem hedges with "in common usage". Confirmed by search that NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 contains neither acronym, so nothing in the item is attributed to it. The distractors are checked against sources: o2 names the RPO and RTO, whose glossary definitions are data loss and elapsed recovery time and which are targets rather than observed averages; o3 is retention; o4 is failover and failback timing. All three whys are true and none is also correct.

items.stem: Backup tapes are stored in a fireproof safe in the same building as the servers. Which requirement remains unmet?

options.text: Off-site storage, because one physical event could still destroy both.
options.why: Distance is the requirement, and a safe in the same building provides none.

options.text: Media diversity, because tape is a single medium.
options.why: Media type is a separate requirement from location and is not what the safe fails.

options.text: Restore testing, because the tapes have not been read back.
options.why: Testing is a real obligation but is not the one the storage location bears on.

options.text: Retention, because a safe does not enforce an expiry schedule.
options.why: Expiry is a policy matter independent of where media is kept.

items.rationale: The requirement is keeping copies or capacity far enough away that one physical event cannot destroy both. Fire resistance raises the threshold but does not create distance — flood, building collapse or a site-wide loss defeats it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "It is good business practice to store backed-up data offsite", and the CISA paper's third clause is "Store 1 copy offsite (e.g., outside your home or business facility)" — a safe in the same building supplies no distance. o2 is false here: tape is a media-diversity point, separate from location. o3 is a real but different obligation. o4 is false; expiry is policy, not a property of the container. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: A facility holds installed, running hardware and the most recent backup already loaded, needing only the data written since that backup before it can take over. Which tier is it?

options.text: A hot site.
options.why: Equipped and loaded with the latest backup, needing only the delta since, is the defining description.

options.text: A mirrored site.
options.why: That tier carries continuously mirrored real-time data and needs no catch-up at all.

options.text: A warm site.
options.why: That holds hardware but not current data, which must be restored before it can serve.

options.text: A cold site.
options.why: That provides space, power and environmental control only, with no hardware in place.

items.rationale: The tiers are separated by how much is already in place. A hot site is fully equipped with the most recent backup loaded and needs only the data written since. Real-time continuous mirroring belongs to the separate and more expensive mirrored site — a distinction that is easy to lose and is exactly where this question sits.

verification.reasoning: Key holds, and the stem is drawn near-verbatim from NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1: "Hot sites should have the most recent version of backed-up data loaded, requiring only updating with data since the last backup." I first recorded this as unsourced after reading only the section 3.4.3 summary list, where the hot site is described just as "configured with the necessary system hardware"; the data sentence is in the chapter 5 alternate-site discussion. o2 is false and its why is verbatim correct: "Mirrored Sites are fully redundant facilities with automated real-time information mirroring." o3 is false — a warm site's "equipment is not loaded with the software or data required to operate the system". o4 is false — a cold site has "basic infrastructure and environmental controls available... but no equipment or telecommunications established or in place".

items.stem: Moving from a hot site to a cold site has which pair of effects?

options.text: Cost falls and recovery time rises.
options.why: Less standing capability is cheaper to hold and slower to bring into service.

options.text: Cost falls and recovery time falls.
options.why: Both cannot improve; the saving is paid for in recovery speed.

options.text: Cost rises and recovery time falls.
options.why: That is the direction of travel toward a hot site, not away from one.

options.text: Cost is unchanged and only tolerable data loss rises.
options.why: Site tier drives cost and recovery time; data loss is bounded by copy frequency instead.

items.rationale: Cost falls and recovery time rises as you move from hot to cold. The tier is a purchase of readiness, and readiness is what shortens the outage — so the two move in opposite directions by construction.

verification.reasoning: Key holds against Table 3-3, Sample Alternate Site Criteria: Cold Site cost Low and setup time Long; Warm Site Medium and Medium; Hot Site Medium/High and Short. Moving hot to cold therefore lowers cost and raises recovery time. o2 and o3 name the impossible and the reversed directions respectively and are false. o4 is false: the document ties tolerable data loss to the RPO and backup frequency, not to site tier. No distractor is also correct.

items.stem: What does a disaster recovery drill establish that restore testing does not?

options.text: That the people involved can execute the plan and know their roles.
options.why: A drill exercises the procedure and the participants, not only the artefact.

options.text: That the backup media can be read back successfully.
options.why: That is what restore testing establishes on its own.

options.text: That the recovery point objective is being met.
options.why: Tolerable data loss is evidenced by copy frequency rather than by a rehearsal.

options.text: That the off-site copies are far enough from the primary.
options.why: Geographic separation is a property of where copies sit, not something a drill measures.

items.rationale: A drill is a rehearsed exercise — full failover or tabletop — proving the plan works and that people know their roles. Restore testing proves one artefact can be read back. The axis is scope: an artefact versus the procedure and the people around it.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 separates the two: testing "validates recovery capabilities" while "training prepares recovery personnel for plan activation and exercising the plan identifies planning gaps", and tabletop exercises have personnel "discuss their roles during an emergency". o2 is what restore testing alone establishes. o3 is false — the recovery point follows from copy frequency. o4 is false; separation is a property of where copies sit. Each why is true and none of the three answers the stem.

items.stem: A team gathers to walk through the recovery plan verbally, without touching production systems. What is this?

options.text: A tabletop drill, which is a legitimate form of exercise.
options.why: A drill may be a full failover or a tabletop walkthrough; both rehearse the plan.

options.text: Not a drill at all, because no systems were actually failed over to the standby.
options.why: Restricting the term to full failover excludes a recognised and useful exercise form.

options.text: Restore testing conducted at low cost.
options.why: No backup was read back, which is what that practice requires.

options.text: A failback rehearsal for the standby site.
options.why: Nothing was switched over, so there is no return leg being practised.

items.rationale: A drill is a rehearsed exercise proving the plan works and that people know their roles, and it may be a full failover or a tabletop. The tabletop form finds gaps in sequencing, contact details and decision rights at a fraction of the cost and risk.

verification.reasoning: Key holds. NIST SP 800-34 Rev. 1 lists tabletop exercises as a recognised exercise type: "discussion-based exercises where personnel meet in a classroom setting or in breakout groups to discuss their roles during an emergency", explicitly one that "does not involve deploying equipment or other resources". o2 is therefore false and is the documented misconception. o3 is false because no backup was read back. o4 is false because nothing was switched over. No distractor is also correct.
